concept.name: MA model
concept.definition: A time-series model in which the current value is a constant plus a linear combination of the current and q past white-noise innovations. Despite the name, it is not a smoothing average of the series but a regression on unobserved past shocks, and it is always stationary.
concept.intuition: An MA model says shocks linger for exactly q periods and then vanish: today's value reflects today's surprise plus fading echoes of the last q surprises.
concept.mechanics: An MA(q) model X_t = mu + A_t - theta_1*A_{t-1} - ... - theta_q*A_{t-q} cannot be fit by ordinary least squares because the A terms are unobserved, so iterative nonlinear (maximum likelihood) estimation is used. Its ACF cuts off after lag q while its PACF decays, the mirror image of AR behavior.
concept.formula: X_t = mu + A_t - theta_1*A_{t-1} - theta_2*A_{t-2} - ... - theta_q*A_{t-q}, with A_t white-noise innovations and q the model order.
concept.failure_modes: Estimation is numerically harder than AR because innovations are latent; non-invertible parameterizations make forecasts unstable. MA structure cannot capture momentum-like dependence on lagged levels.
concept.misconceptions: That an MA model is the same as a moving-average smoothing of prices used in technical analysis; the MA(q) time-series model weights past shocks, not past observed values.
concept.example: An MA(1) for daily returns says today's return depends on today's news shock plus a fraction of yesterday's shock, so the ACF is nonzero only at lag 1.

citations.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, Section 6.4.4.4 Common Approaches to Univariate Time Series
